## The case

You are the data analyst on a small study. Your client is the channel manager at a small creator
agency that represents about a dozen Twitch streamers. The agency is about to pitch a sponsor on
how engaged its streamers' chats are. Before the pitch, the manager wants three questions
answered with data:

1. Does chat in gaming channels look different from chat in non-gaming channels?
2. Does a bigger audience change how people write?
3. How much of chat is reaction (an emote, a cheer, a single word) and how much is commentary?

**The problem.** The data you have been handed cannot answer any of these yet. It is two raw
tables: one of chat messages, and one of stream snapshots (what each channel was streaming and
how many people were watching). The time on every message is a thirteen-digit number. Nothing
connects a message to the size of its audience. No column says which channels are gaming
channels. And no dataset records whether a message is a reaction: someone has to read the
messages and decide.

**Your job.** Turn the two raw tables into one clean table that can answer the manager's
questions, and save it as `twitch_analysis.RDS`. The next two assignments, Describing Data and
Inferencing Data, both start from that file. Everything you tell the client later rests on the
table you build here.

## Your assignment

Work through the parts in order. Each one fixes one thing that stands between the raw data and
the client's questions.

| Part | What you do | Why the client needs it |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Read thirty chat messages and code each one as reaction or commentary | Question 3 needs a variable that only a person can make |
| 1 | Load the two raw tables | You have to see what you were handed |
| 2 | Look for empty cells and other traps | You find the problems before they reach the client's numbers |
| 3 | Turn the timestamps into real times and measure each message's length | "How people write" needs a number, and the join needs a time |
| 4 | Join the stream and channel information onto every message | Questions 1 and 2 need the channel type and audience size on each message |
| 5 | Join your thirty codes onto the table | Question 3 needs your codes beside the other variables |
| 6 | Count the missing values and write what you did with them | The client should know what was left out, and why |
| 7 | Save the finished table | The next two assignments start from this file |
| 8 | MC 501 only: three reviewer-facing comments | A reviewer can check the decisions behind the table |

The code sits in gray boxes called chunks. In every part, the work is the same three moves:

1. Replace each blank, shown as `___`, with the code it needs.
2. Run the chunk: click **Run Cell** at the top left of its gray box.
3. Compare what R prints with **What you should see**, the text right under the chunk.

Not sure what a blank needs? [Help and reference](#help), the last section, lists the R Companion
menu that writes each step and links the cheat sheets.

Where the worksheet says **Write:**, type your answer under *Your answer:*, in your own words.
Run the chunks in order, because each one uses what the one before it made. Start at **Setup**,

## Setup

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)     # the tools for every data step
library(janitor)       # clean_names(), for the coding sheet's column names
library(v2v)           # the course package: the Twitch data and helpers
options(scipen = 10)  # long numbers such as timestamps print in full; p-values keep the usual form
```

**What you should see:** a list of attached packages and a line naming the `v2v` version. The
lines about "conflicts" are normal.

## Part 0: Hand-code thirty messages

The manager's third question is about reactions, and no dataset has a reaction column. You make
one by reading thirty messages and coding each by hand.

### Task 0.1: Draw the coding sample

Everyone in the class codes the same thirty messages: fifteen from `bobross` (a non-gaming
channel) and fifteen from `giantwaffle` (a gaming channel).

```{r}
#| label: draw-sample
set.seed(20261113)  # the class seed: everyone draws the same thirty

coding_sample <- twitch_chat(channels = c("bobross", "giantwaffle")) %>%  # keep the two channels first
  group_by(channel) %>%                                                    # one draw per channel
  slice_sample(n = 15) %>%                                                 # 15 from each
  ungroup()

coding_sample %>%
  count(channel)
```

**What you should see:** two rows, `bobross` with `15` and `giantwaffle` with `15`.

### Task 0.2: Write the coding sheet

This saves the thirty messages as your coding sheet, `data/coding-form.csv`. Run this chunk
**once**: click **Run Cell** at its top left. Rendering the worksheet skips this chunk, so it
never wipes out the codes you type into the file.

```{r}
#| label: write-form
#| eval: false
dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)  # makes the data folder if it is not there yet

coding_sample %>%
  select(id, channel, message) %>%   # the key, the channel, and the text to code
  write_csv("data/coding-form.csv")  # run once; rendering skips this chunk
```

**What you should see:** `coding-form.csv` in the `data` folder in the **Explorer** panel, with
30 rows.

### Task 0.3: Code each message by hand

Code one variable, `reaction_only`, for all thirty messages, using this codebook entry.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Variable** | `reaction_only` |
| **Conceptual definition** | A message that only reacts to the stream or the chat, without putting a thought of its own into words. |
| **Operational definition** | Code **1 (reaction)** when the message holds nothing but emotes, laughter, a cheer, a single exclamation, or a word stretched into a sound. Code **0 (commentary)** when it holds at least one word or phrase that comments, asks, answers, or tells. |
| **Rule 1** | An emote name counts as a reaction even when it looks like a word (`CoolStoryBob`, `PepoDance`, `KappaRoss`, `LULW`). |
| **Rule 2** | A single cheer or exclamation is a reaction (`GOOD`, `xD`, `100`, `gg`). |
| **Rule 3** | A word stretched into a sound is a reaction (`Booooohiss`, `TREEEEES`). |
| **Rule 4** | Two or more words that say something are commentary, however short (`BIG TREE`, `rip devil`). |
| **Rule 5** | One word plus emotes is commentary only if the word says something about the stream or the chat; otherwise it is a reaction. |
| **When unsure** | Code 0 and write why in `coder_notes`. |

Open `data/coding-form.csv` in a spreadsheet (Excel, Google Sheets, or Numbers). Add two columns
headed `reaction_only` and `coder_notes`. Type `0` or `1` in every row of `reaction_only`. Save
the file **as a CSV with the same name**. Leave the `id` column exactly as it is.

To code in the R Companion's data viewer instead, follow the guide *Read and Code Data in the
Data Viewer*:
[MC 451](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/guides/mc451/05-data-viewer-and-coding-columns.html)
or [MC 501](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/guides/mc501/05-data-viewer-and-coding-columns.html).

## Part 1: Load the two tables

These are the two raw tables you were handed. The Twitch data ships inside the course package,
`v2v`, so there is no file to find.

### Task 1.1: Load from the course package

```{r}
#| label: load
chat <- ___()        # one row per chat message
streams <- ___()  # one row per snapshot of a stream
```

**What you should see:** nothing in the console. `chat` and `streams` appear in the Workspace
panel.

### Task 1.2: First look

```{r}
#| label: glimpse
glimpse(chat)
glimpse(streams)
```

**What you should see:** `Rows: 35,267` and `Columns: 5` for `chat`, then `Rows: 32,276` and
`Columns: 6` for `streams`. Look at `date`: it is a run of thirteen-digit numbers. Task 3.1
turns them into times.

## Part 2: Diagnose

Before you fix anything, find out what is wrong with the data. A problem you miss here ends up
in the numbers the client reads.

### Task 2.1: Missing values

`is.na()` asks, for every row, whether a cell is empty. Count the messages with no text and the
snapshots with no category.

```{r}
#| label: missing-raw
chat %>%
  count(is.na(message))  # TRUE = the message is empty

streams %>%
  count(is.na(game))     # TRUE = the snapshot has no category
```

**What you should see:** for `chat`, `TRUE` with `4`. For `streams`, `TRUE` with `96`. Part 6
comes back to these.

### Task 2.2: Two columns called `id`

Nothing to run here. Both tables have a column named `id`, and the two mean different things: a
chat `id` names a message and a stream `id` names a snapshot. Joining the two tables on `id`
would run without an error and pair messages with unrelated snapshots. So the tables join on
channel and time (Task 4.1). Your coding sheet joins on `id` (Task 5.3), because its `id` is the
chat `id`.

### Task 2.3: Categories

```{r}
#| label: categories
streams %>%
  count(game, sort = TRUE)  # snapshots per category, most common first

chat %>%
  distinct(channel) %>%     # one row per channel
  nrow()                    # how many channels
```

**What you should see:** a table that starts `Art`, `Fortnite`, `Just Chatting`, then `[1] 50`.

## Part 3: Fix

The client asked how people write. That needs each message's length as a number, and a time on
each message that R can read.

### Task 3.1: Make the timestamps readable

Give both tables a `ts` column holding a real date and time.

```{r}
#| label: timestamps
chat <- chat %>%
  mutate(ts = ___(date / 1000))  # milliseconds -> seconds -> date and time

streams <- streams %>%
  mutate(ts = ___(date / 1000))

chat %>%
  summarize(first = min(ts), last = max(ts))  # the first and last message
```

The blank is the lubridate function that turns a count of seconds into a date and time.

**What you should see:** a one-row table: `first` is `2018-11-18 21:55:27` and `last` is
`2018-11-24 18:20:23`. Six days in November 2018.

### Task 3.2: Message length

Count the characters in each message.

```{r}
#| label: length
chat <- chat %>%
  mutate(message_length = ___(___))  # characters per message

chat %>%
  select(message, message_length) %>%
  slice_head(n = 3)
```

**What you should see:** three messages with lengths `23`, `441`, and `8`.

## Part 4: Join

The client's first two questions compare channels by type and by audience size. Those facts sit
in other tables, so you join them onto every message.

### Task 4.1: Match each message to its stream

A stream snapshot is taken about once a minute. Give each message the snapshot taken at or just
before it, on the same channel.

```{r}
#| label: join-streams
snapshots <- streams %>%
  select(channel, snapshot_ts = ts, game, viewers)  # four columns; ts renamed on the way

chat_streams <- chat %>%
  ___(
    snapshots,
    by = join_by(channel, closest(ts >= snapshot_ts))  # same channel, nearest earlier snapshot
  )

nrow(chat_streams)                     # the join must not add or lose rows
chat_streams %>%
  count(no_snapshot = is.na(viewers))  # messages with no earlier snapshot
```

The blank is the join that keeps every row of `chat`.

**What you should see:** `[1] 35267`, then `FALSE` with `35256` and `TRUE` with `11`. Eleven
messages came before their channel's first snapshot, so they have nothing to match.

### Task 4.2: Join the channel labels onto the messages

The course package ships a table with one row per channel. It says whether the channel counts as
gaming (`is_gaming`, and the same thing in words, `channel_type`) and how big its audience is
(`viewer_band`). Run `?twitch_channels` in the R console to read how those labels were decided.

```{r}
#| label: channel-labels
channels <- ___()  # the lookup table: one row per channel

channels %>%
  count(is_gaming)   # channels, not messages

# MC 501 only: reviewer-facing comment 1 goes here (see Part 8).
analysis <- chat_streams %>%
  left_join(channels, by = "___")  # YOUR TURN: replace this comment with one naming the key and why

analysis %>%
  count(is_gaming)   # messages
```

**What you should see:** for the channels, `FALSE` with `5`, `TRUE` with `43`, and `NA` with
`2`. For the messages, `FALSE` with `3457`, `TRUE` with `31309`, and `NA` with `501`. The 501
come from the two channels that never recorded a category. An honest `NA` is the right answer.

### Task 4.3: Check the audience bands

`viewer_band` came in with the join. It sorts channels into small, medium, and large audiences,
in that order.

```{r}
#| label: viewer-band
# MC 501 only: reviewer-facing comment 2 goes here (see Part 8).
channels %>%
  count(viewer_band)  # channels per band

analysis %>%
  count(viewer_band)  # messages per band
```

**What you should see:** `small` with `41`, `medium` with `7`, `large` with `2` for the
channels: the large band is two streamers. Then `small` with `27766`, `medium` with `5501`, and
`large` with `2000` for the messages.

### Task 4.4: Check the channel type

`channel_type` says gaming or non-gaming in words. Every later table and test groups by it.

```{r}
#| label: channel-type
analysis %>%
  count(channel_type)  # messages per label, in the factor's order
```

**What you should see:** `gaming` with `31309`, `non-gaming` with `3457`, and `NA` with `501`.

## Part 5: Read your codes back and join them

Your thirty codes from Part 0 answer the client's third question only once they sit in the same
table as everything else.

### Task 5.1: Read the coding sheet

Read your coding sheet into R and tidy its column names.

```{r}
#| label: read-codes
codes <- ___("data/coding-form.csv") %>%  # the form you filled in
  ___()                                 # lowercase, underscores
```

**What you should see:** `Rows: 30` and the column types.

### Task 5.2: Make the codes a labeled factor

`0` and `1` are codes, not amounts. Give them labels that say what they mean.

```{r}
#| label: codes-factor
codes <- codes %>%
  mutate(reaction_only = ___(reaction_only,
                                levels = c(___),
                                labels = c("commentary", "reaction"))) %>%
  select(id, reaction_only)  # only the key and the code; the message text stays in the package data

codes %>%
  count(reaction_only)
```

**What you should see:** two rows that add to `30`, and no `NA` row. With the instructor's codes
it is `commentary` `17` and `reaction` `13`; yours may differ by a few, because five of the
thirty are deliberately borderline.

### Task 5.3: Join the codes onto the analysis table

```{r}
#| label: join-codes
analysis <- analysis %>%
  left_join(codes, by = "___")  # YOUR TURN: replace this comment with one naming the key and why

nrow(analysis)  # still one row per message

analysis %>%
  count(reaction_only)
```

**What you should see:** `[1] 35267`, then your two coded groups adding to `30`, and `NA` with
`35237`. Only your thirty messages carry a code; every other message is `NA` on this variable,
and that is correct.

## Part 6: Missing values

The client will see numbers built from this table. They should know which messages those numbers
leave out. Count the messages missing a value on each column the tests will use.

```{r}
#| label: missing-analysis
analysis %>%
  count(is.na(message_length))  # the four empty messages

analysis %>%
  count(is.na(viewers))         # the eleven messages with no earlier snapshot

analysis %>%
  count(is.na(channel_type))    # the 501 from the two unlabeled channels
```

**What you should see:** `TRUE` with `4`, then `TRUE` with `11`, then `TRUE` with `501`. No
message is missing on two of these at once, so 516 messages carry a missing value in all.

**Write:** how many messages carry a missing value, where each kind comes from, and what you did
with them. Say it as a decision another researcher could check.

Save the finished table as `twitch_analysis.RDS`. Describing Data and Inferencing Data both read
that exact name. An `.RDS` file keeps every column exactly as you built it; a `.csv` would lose
the order of small, medium, and large.

```{r}
#| label: export
# MC 501 only: reviewer-facing comment 3 goes here (see Part 8).
___(analysis, "data/___")  # save

read_rds("data/twitch_analysis.RDS") %>%              # load it back
  nrow()                                              # and count the rows
```

**What you should see:** `[1] 35267`, and `twitch_analysis.RDS` in the `data` folder.

## Part 8: MC 501 only, three reviewer-facing comments

MC 501 adds three comments to the code, each 40 to 100 words, at the three places marked
*MC 501 only* above: the non-gaming list the lookup table applies (Task 4.2), the viewer-band
cutoffs it uses (Task 4.3), and the export (Part 7). Each one names a decision a reviewer could
challenge, the rule you applied, and why you chose it over the alternative. Adopting the
package's list or cutoffs is itself a decision: say why they fit this study, or what you would
change. A comment that says what the code does is not one of the

### If something goes wrong

| Where | What you see | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Any chunk | `object '___' not found` | A blank is still empty in that chunk. Fill it and run the chunk again. |
| Setup | `there is no package called 'janitor'`, or later `could not find function "twitch_channels"` | Run **AURA: Check my setup**, then **Install what is missing**, and run the chunk again. |
| Task 0.1 | Your thirty messages differ from a classmate's | Run the whole chunk again from its first line, so the seed line runs right before the draw. |
| Task 0.2 | `coding-form.csv` was already in `data` | Leave it. It holds the same thirty messages, and your codes are safe. |
| Task 3.1 | The year is in the tens of thousands | The `/ 1000` is missing from the line. |
| Task 5.2 | An `NA` row in the count | A code is something other than `0` or `1`: a blank cell, a space after the number, or a word. Fix it in the coding sheet and run Task 5.1 again. |
| Task 5.3 | The row count went up | The coding sheet has the same `id` twice. |
| Task 5.3 | The coded rows add to fewer than 30 | An `id` in your coding sheet no longer matches a message. Check that the `id` column was not changed when you saved. |

### Key terms

| Term | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Row** | One of the things you study. Here, one row is one chat message. |
| **Variable** | One thing you record about every row, such as a message's length or its channel. Each variable is one column. |
| **Hand-code** | Read each message yourself and record a value for it, following a written rule. The rule is the codebook entry in Task 0.3. |
| **Pipe (`%>%`)** | Read it as "and then": it hands the result of one line to the next line. |
| **Timestamp** | The date and time something happened. In this data it is stored as a count of milliseconds since January 1, 1970. |
| **Missing value (`NA`)** | A cell with nothing in it. R prints `NA`, short for "not available." |
| **Key** | The column two tables share, which tells R which row in one table goes with which row in the other. |
| **Join** | Putting two tables together by matching their keys, so each row picks up the other table's columns. |
| **Factor** | R's way of storing a category (small, medium, large) with its labels in an order you choose. |
| **RDS file** | R's own file format. It saves a table exactly as you built it, factors and times included. |
